results.evidence: Only the Django path adds `**({"assignee_name": assignee_name} ...)`. The author says ingestion-emitted events (created, and reopened/spiking from ingestion) are produced by Rust code that was not touched. Alert delivery inputs also don't carry the name. So many issue events with an assignee still lack it.
For a user the code returns `(user.first_name or user.email)`, i.e. the first name only, not the full/display name. The role branch does return `role.name`.

`_assignee_name` returns None when `assignee is None`, and the property is only added when non-None: `**({"assignee_name": assignee_name} if assignee_name is not None else {})`. `assignee` is likewise omitted when there is no assignment.
`assignee_property` and `_current_assignee_property` are unchanged, so the same compact JSON string is emitted, with int user ids and str role ids.
`(user.first_name or user.email)` falls back to the email when the first name is empty.
No assignee email property is added anywhere in the patch. Only `assignee_name` is emitted.

The user lookup is `User.objects.filter(id=parsed["id"])` with no organization-membership check. No check compares the current assignee with the one on the event. `extra.get("assignee", current_assignee)` uses the event's assignee to look up the name.

The new docs section says both properties are absent when the issue is unassigned. It gives `assignee` as a JSON string, "holds an id only; use it for exact-match filters, not for display". It says `assignee_name` is "the readable name to show" and to use it in message text.

result:
Lifecycle events that Django emits now carry an `assignee_name` next to `assignee`. I haven't run any tests or added one. Events emitted by the ingestion service (created, and reopened or spiking when they come from ingestion) still don't include it, because that emitter is Rust code I didn't touch.

- **Name lookup:** `products/error_tracking/backend/logic/lifecycle_events.py` looks up the name from the `assignee` value. For a user it uses their first name, falling back to their email. For a role it uses the role's name, looked up only within the issue's organization. The existing `assignee` string and the `previous_assignee` string are unchanged.
- **Unassigned issues:** `assignee_name` is left out, the same as `assignee`. If the user or role no longer exists, it is also left out.
- **Which events:** the name follows whatever `assignee` the event carries. An assigned event names the new assignee. Other manual events, such as a resolve, name the issue's current assignee.
- **Filters:** I added `assignee_name` to `LIFECYCLE_PROPERTY_KEYS` in `backend/temporal/alerts/filtering.py`. A filter on it can then be decided without the exception's properties.
- **AI docs:** `skills/authoring-error-tracking-alerts/references/event-triggers.md` has a new "Assignee properties" section. It describes the shape of `assignee` and `previous_assignee`, says `assignee_name` is the field to use for display, and notes which events don't set it.

Alert deliveries (the Slack-style alert messages) don't get the name, since their inputs only carry the `assignee` string. Adding it there would mean extending `AlertDeliveryWorkflowInputs`.

+## Assignee properties
+
+Events emitted from manual changes (assigned, unassigned, resolved, manual reopen and so on) carry the assignee of the issue.
+`assignee_name` is not set on `_created`, or on `_reopened` and `_spiking` events that come from ingestion. When the issue is unassigned, both properties are absent.
+
+- `event.properties.assignee` — a JSON string such as `{"type":"user","id":1234}` or `{"type":"role","id":"<role uuid>"}`.
+  It holds an id only; use it for exact-match filters, not for display.
+- `event.properties.assignee_name` — the readable name to show: the user's first name (or email if unset), or the role's name.
+- `event.properties.previous_assignee` — on `_unassigned`, the same JSON string for who held the issue before.
+
+Use `assignee_name` in message text, for example `Assigned to {event.properties.assignee_name}`.
+Do not guess a name from `assignee`.
